SEPA Instant allows near-instant (<10s) euro transfers any time. Greek banks have joined this scheme, enabling customers to send up to €15,000 immediately, 24/7, to other EU recipients. It is cleared via TIPS. Adoption in Greece is growing as banks upgrade to this service.

As an EU member, Greece uses the TARGET2 (now T2) RTGS system for euro-denominated high-value payments. The Bank of Greece settles interbank transfers (large-value or cross-border) via TARGET2, with immediate finality in central bank money. T2 processes vast volumes (near euro-area GDP every few days) [oai_citation:42‡bundesbank.de].

Under SEPA, Greek banks exchange euro credit transfer orders through batch clearing (SEPA Credit Transfer). These include domestic and cross-border payments (salaries, supplier payments, etc.). They settle periodically via TARGET. SEPA CT is the default for euro payments in Greece.
TARGET2 is used by Greece as part of the Eurosystem for real-time gross settlement of large-value payments.

Greek retailers and consumers predominantly use international card schemes like Visa, Mastercard and AMEX. Although there is no separate Greek-branded card scheme, banks and merchants are linked via the European 'SEPA Card Clearing' system for euro card payments. Banks use Visa/Mastercard processing and link them through the TARGET2 platform for settlement in euro.
Mobile payment system
Mobile wallet

SICOF is Guatemala’s interbank check-clearing and ACH system ("Cámara de Compensación Bancaria"). Banks send checks and small transfers to the clearinghouse, which nets obligations and settles them the next day. This system supports retail payments, payroll, and bill payments, improving efficiency by replacing physical check exchange.

Banco de Guatemala operates SIGA (Sistema de Intermediación de Pagos), an RTGS system for interbank settlements. All large-value and urgent transfers between banks in GTQ are settled immediately through SIGA in central bank money. This forms the backbone of Guatemala’s payment infrastructure [oai_citation:47‡banguat.gob.gt].
Primary payment method

GIM-UEMOA is a regional payment scheme and switch uniting banks across WAEMU (Senegal, Bénin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Togo, Guinea-Bissau). It enables cross-border acceptance of EMV cards and mobile payments. GIM-UEMOA operates an electronic payment platform for its ~150 member financial institutions, promoting interoperability and financial inclusion in the eight-country region [oai_citation:57‡african.business].

Orange Money operates in Guinea-Bissau, offering mobile wallet services. Customers can send/receive funds via USSD or app, pay bills, and cash in/out at Orange agents. It is one of the key digital channels in the country’s payment ecosystem.
SICA-UEMOA supports instant payments for over 90 financial institutions in WAEMU, including Guinea-Bissau.

As part of the West African Economic and Monetary Union, Guinea-Bissau uses the SICA (Système Interbancaire de Compensation Automatisé) for retail clearing. All banks in WAEMU send bulk payments (transfers <50M XOF, checks, bills) to SICA-UEMOA, which nets and settles them in centralized cycles [oai_citation:55‡payrollhq.blob.core.windows.net]. This regional ACH handles most routine bank transfers and check clearing.
Mobile wallet

G-RTGS is Guyana’s central bank RTGS system for real-time, irrevocable settlement of large-value interbank transactions. Launched in early 2021 [oai_citation:1‡bankofguyana.org.gy], it is operated by the Bank of Guyana. Payments settle individually and immediately between participants’ central bank accounts, eliminating settlement risk. Participating banks can pledge securities as collateral to access intraday liquidity [oai_citation:2‡bankofguyana.org.gy]. The system underpins the national payment infrastructure and supports high-value transfers among commercial banks and government entities. Liquid funds management and collateralization are integral to its operation [oai_citation:3‡bankofguyana.org.gy].

The main mobile money service in Guyana is offered by Guyana Telephone and Telegraph (GTT) under the brand “Mobicash” or similar. It functions as an electronic wallet allowing users to send/receive money and pay bills via mobile phone without a bank account [oai_citation:15‡cherieblairfoundation.org] [oai_citation:16‡moncashdfs.com]. As of 2022, this service had over 2 million registered users in Haiti (similar platform) [oai_citation:17‡moncashdfs.com], suggesting strong adoption. In Guyana’s largely cash-based economy, mobile money provides convenient digital payments for consumers and merchants. The system is networked through a country-wide agent network for cash in/out. Transactions include P2P transfers, merchant payments, utility bill and bill payments, and airtime top-ups. GTT, acting under Central Bank guidelines, integrates mobile transfers with bank accounts via the EFT/ACH or future RTGS rails. The service is available 24/7 and supports interoperability with banking channels. GTT’s initiative, often supported by financial inclusion programs [oai_citation:18‡cherieblairfoundation.org], is considered a key tool for extending financial services into rural regions.

Guyana’s card payments are primarily handled via international networks (Visa/MasterCard) and a national ATM network. All commercial banks are interconnected through a switch (Guyana National Clearing Card) for ATM and POS transactions, which route card payments to issuing banks for settlement. The Central Bank oversees the infrastructure’s reliability. A domestic debit/credit card scheme operates under Visa/MasterCard licenses. Transaction clearing for cards ultimately settles via the EFT or RTGS system. Contactless and QR payments are growing but still small. Overall, card usage is modest compared to cash, but expanding slowly as infrastructure improves.

Guyana’s EFT system is a multichannel automated clearing house for retail payments, operated under Bank of Guyana regulation [oai_citation:5‡bankofguyana.org.gy] [oai_citation:6‡bankofguyana.org.gy]. Launched in November 2018 [oai_citation:7‡bankofguyana.org.gy], it processes batch credit and debit transfers (e.g. payroll, utility payments, loan payments) between bank accounts via POS, ATM, internet, phone or other electronic means [oai_citation:8‡bankofguyana.org.gy] [oai_citation:9‡bch.hn]. EFT participants include all commercial banks and financial institutions. Transactions are processed in multiple daily batches, with credit and debit instructions netted among banks. EFT replaced paper-based transactions (e.g. cheques) with faster electronic processing [oai_citation:10‡bankofguyana.org.gy] [oai_citation:11‡bch.hn]. It is administered by the interbank processing center (Ceproban) under central bank oversight. EFT has significantly reduced cheque usage and improved payment speeds [oai_citation:12‡bankofguyana.org.gy].

Operated by the Bank of Guyana, the EFT rail supports bank-to-bank transfers submitted over secure online channels and settled across participants’ reserve accounts. It is the backbone used by commercial banks for salary processing, government disbursements and retail credit transfers during business hours.

Licensed as an electronic-money institution under BoG Draft E-Money Regulation, MMG+ links wallets to any feature-phone via USSD or app, enabling cash-in/out at agents nationwide and instant wallet-to-wallet transfers in Guyanese dollars.

Tigo Money is an electronic wallet service launched by Millicom (Tigo) in Honduras. It allows users to send and receive money, pay utility bills, make purchases at partner merchants, and access remittances via mobile phones. Customers register with an authorized retailer to open a wallet linked to their mobile number. Funds can be deposited or withdrawn at Tigo agent locations. Tigo Money transactions are processed instantly, and underlying settlement between banks uses the ACH Pronto/RTGS infrastructure. By 2017, the user base grew from 1.0M to 1.5M wallets [oai_citation:50‡afi-global.org] (50% growth in two years). It continues to grow, aided by simple KYC and interoperability with banks (transfer to bank accounts via ACH). Tigo Money agents (shops) provide nationwide coverage, including rural areas. The service is regulated by the central bank under mobile money regulations (Acuerdo 01/2016) [oai_citation:51‡afi-global.org].

ACH Pronto is Honduras’s automated clearing house (clearing and settlement of retail payments). Managed by the Centro de Procesamiento Interbancario (Ceproban, owned by the banks) [oai_citation:39‡bch.hn], it processes high-volume, low-value credit and debit transfers in batch mode. Typical ACH transactions include payroll deposits, pension/disbursements, supplier payments, tax payments, utility bill collections, loan collections, etc. Instructions are submitted by banks and cleared in defined cycles. Participants include all commercial banks and financial institutions regulated by the Honduran Banking and Securities Commission. The ACH accelerates fund availability and reduces costs by eliminating physical checks [oai_citation:40‡bch.hn] [oai_citation:41‡bch.hn]. It has become the standard mechanism for mass payments (e.g. salaries, government payments) in Honduras. Settlement of ACH net positions is performed via the BCH-TR RTGS [oai_citation:42‡bch.hn].aspx#:~:text=,ACH%20Pronto). The system operates intraday with multiple settlement cycles each day [oai_citation:43‡bch.hn].

Honduras maintains a centralized electronic cheque clearing house (CCECh) for processing interbank cheque payments. Cheques presented at banks are exchanged electronically through CCECh, which nets payments and settles the balances. While usage of cheques is declining, CCECh ensures legacy cheque instruments are reliably processed. The BCH-TR RTGS system is used to settle net positions from the cheque clearing twice daily [oai_citation:44‡bch.hn].aspx#:~:text=,ACH%20Pronto). Participants are all banks issuing or clearing cheques. CCECh provides a structured, automated replacement for manual cheque exchange, reducing float time and processing costs. Over time, it is being overtaken by digital transfers, but it remains part of the payment infrastructure.

The Sistema de Interconexión de Pagos (SIPA) is a regional payment platform linking Honduras with Central America and the Dominican Republic [oai_citation:46‡bch.hn]. Operated by Banco Central de Honduras, SIPA settles cross-border USD transfers for remittances, trade payments, and interbank transfers among participating banks. Direct participants include the central banks of the region; Honduran commercial banks join as indirect participants (currently eight Honduran banks) [oai_citation:47‡bch.hn]. SIPA consolidates operations regionally into one platform, with fixed low fees and enhanced settlement speed [oai_citation:48‡bch.hn]. It supports remittance inflows/outflows and regional commerce. Volumes have been growing as remittances to/from Honduras expand. SIPA complements domestic clearing by providing a secure 24/7 inter-country settlement layer (settlement in BCH-TR).
Private bank-owned ACH that processes consumer and SME credit transfers 5 am-10 pm daily with near-instant settlement; reforms approved to open access to cooperatives.

Tengo is a digital payment platform launched by BanProvivi (a Honduran state-owned second-tier bank) as an electronic wallet. It enables peer-to-peer transfers, bill payments, and QR-code payments. Launched around 2018, Tengo was intended to promote financial inclusion. Users can top up their Tengo account and transact via smartphone. Payments clear instantly via the interconnected ACH/RTGS systems. Adoption has been growing more slowly than Tigo Money due to later entry and initial interoperability barriers. Nonetheless, Tengo adds competition to the mobile money market. It follows central bank guidelines for e-money issuance. (No official transaction figures are publicly reported.)
Under 2022 regulation, INDELs issue store-value, provide P2P transfers and merchant QR acceptance via smartphone apps; supervised by CNBS.

The Sistema Banco Central de Honduras en Tiempo Real (BCH-TR) is the country’s RTGS platform, implemented by Banco Central de Honduras. Launched on March 4, 2013 [oai_citation:35‡bch.hn].aspx#:~:text=Es%20el%20sis%20tema%20de,4%20de%20marzo%20del%202013), BCH-TR settles high-value, time-critical interbank payments in real time, continuously (transaction-by-transaction). It is administered by the central bank and is the backbone of Honduras’s payment system. The RTGS handles interbank transfers, government payments, securities settlement and also nets and settles other clearing systems (ACH Pronto, check clearing, foreign exchange trades, etc.) [oai_citation:36‡bch.hn].aspx#:~:text=Operaciones%20que%20se%20Liquidan%20en,el%20Sistema). BCH-TR uses prefunded accounts at the central bank with liquidity management features (intraday credit against collateral). Participation is open to all financial institutions and eligible public entities. Because it provides immediate finality, BCH-TR reduces settlement risk for large-value transactions and supports monetary policy implementation [oai_citation:37‡bch.hn].aspx#:~:text=Es%20un%20sistema%20de%20liquidaci%C3%B3n,tiempo%20real%20y%20sin%20neteo).

sistemas.nome: RTGS/CD (Sistema de Liquidación Bruta en Tiempo Real)
sistemas.descricao: Launched 2013 to replace manual high-value clearing. Operated by Banco Central de Honduras (BCH), the system settles MX positional balances, securities and FX legs.
Automated clearing house
Mobile wallet
Croatia’s large-value RTGS system via the Eurosystem
sistemas.detalhes: Since adopting the euro in 2023, Croatia’s high-value payments settle through TARGET-HR, the national component of the Eurosystem’s TARGET2/T2 RTGS (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=Payment%20systems%20are%20funds%20transfer,HR%2C%20EuroNCS%20and%20EuroNCSInst) (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=After%20the%20introduction%20of%20the,the%20TARGET%20platform%20in%20euro). This replaced the former Croatian Large Value Payment System (CLVPS) for kuna, fully migrating large-value settlements to euro central bank money (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=After%20the%20introduction%20of%20the,the%20TARGET%20platform%20in%20euro). TARGET-HR processes real-time gross settlements for interbank transfers, securities, and instant payments (via TIPS). All Croatian banks participate, making adoption universal. It ensures immediate, final settlement of large-value and urgent euro transfers.

sistemas.descricao: Domestic SEPA clearing house for Euro credit transfers and direct debits
sistemas.detalhes: EuroNCS is Croatia’s retail payment clearing system for SEPA Credit Transfers (SCT) and Direct Debits (SDD) in euro (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=EuroNCS%C2%A0,SDD%29%20payment%20transactions) (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=With%20the%20introduction%20of%20the,system%20to%20the%20EuroNCS%20system). Operational since 2016, it initially cleared only euro transactions, and with euro adoption it took over all former kuna retail payments (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=The%20EuroNCS%20payment%20system%20became,SEPA%20credit%20transfers%20in%20euro). EuroNCS provides batch net settlement of interbank transfers, interoperating with other European clearing houses to ensure full SEPA reach (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=payment%20system%20to%20the%20EuroNCS,system). All banks are connected through the system (operated by Fina), making usage widespread. It processes millions of payments monthly (salaries, bills, etc.) with next-day settlement.

sistemas.descricao: Real-time instant credit transfer system (SCT Inst) in Euro
sistemas.detalhes: EuroNCSInst is Croatia’s 24/7 instant payment system, enabling SEPA Instant Credit Transfers (SCT Inst) between banks within seconds (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=match%20at%20L868%20EuroNCSInst%20is,SEPA%20Instant%20Credit%20Transfer%2C%20SCTInst) (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=EuroNCSInst%20is%20a%20payment%20system,SEPA%20Instant%20Credit%20Transfer%2C%20SCTInst). Launched in October 2020 (originally in kuna as NCSInst) and converted to euro in 2023, it allows immediate transfers up to EUR 100,000. The instant clearing is operated by Fina and integrated with the TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) service for pan-European reach (https://www.hnb.hr/en/core-functions/payment-system/payment-systems#:~:text=Croatia%2C%20the%20NCSInst%20payment%20system,instant%20payment%20transactions%20in%20euro). Most major banks offer instant payments via this system, and usage is growing as consumers and businesses embrace real-time transfers around the clock.

sistemas.descricao: Visa/Mastercard card payments with widespread acceptance in Croatia
sistemas.detalhes: Croatians commonly use debit and credit cards (Visa, Mastercard, Diners Club, etc.) for cashless payments. The country has about 1.9 million payment cards in circulation (as of 2023) (https://cyprus-mail.com/2024/08/02/cyprus-sees-e129-billion-in-cashless-transactions-in-second-half-of-2023#:~:text=technology%2C%20with%20over%2074%20per,per%20cent%20in%20the%20eurozone), and card usage is high in retail and ecommerce. Most card transactions are processed by JCC Payment Systems, the national card processor, which handles merchant acquiring and card clearing (https://www.ecb.europa.eu/paym/pol/systems/html/index.da.html#:~:text=EuroNKS%20). Contactless card payments are very popular – by 2023, 74% of ATMs and a majority of POS terminals supported contactless cards (https://cyprus-mail.com/2024/08/02/cyprus-sees-e129-billion-in-cashless-transactions-in-second-half-of-2023#:~:text=Furthermore%2C%20betting%20services%20ranked%20as,payments%20made%20with%20Cypriot%20cards). Card payments account for a large share of non-cash transactions alongside SEPA transfers.

sistemas.descricao: Domestic fintech mobile payment apps for P2P and merchant payments
sistemas.detalhes: Croatia has several popular mobile wallet apps. **Keks Pay**, launched by Erste Bank, allows instant peer-to-peer transfers via phone contacts and is widely used among young adults. **Aircash** is another Croatian e-wallet enabling money transfers, bill payments, and even cryptocurrency purchase. These services link to users’ bank accounts or cards to facilitate quick payments. While not an official national system, they complement the banking infrastructure. Adoption of mobile wallets is growing, contributing to a cashless culture (Croatia has over 70% smartphone penetration). Many users leverage these apps for splitting bills and online purchases.

sistemas.descricao: The CLVPS was Croatia’s RTGS for high-value transactions in the domestic currency (Croatian kuna). It settled interbank payments in real time and gross basis, handling monetary policy operations, cash supply transactions, securities settlement, and final settlement for retail systems [oai_citation:22‡hnb.hr] [oai_citation:23‡hnb.hr]. Operated by the Croatian National Bank (CNB), CLVPS used the SWIFT network and FIN Copy service for message exchange [oai_citation:24‡hnb.hr]. Participants included the CNB, all licensed banks, the development bank and the securities depository [oai_citation:25‡hnb.hr]. CLVPS ensured immediate finality for each transaction, queuing payments if insufficient funds until liquidity was available or end-of-day [oai_citation:26‡hnb.hr] [oai_citation:27‡hnb.hr]. This system was discontinued in January 2023 when Croatia adopted the euro and migrated to the Eurosystem’s TARGET-HR platform [oai_citation:28‡hnb.hr].

Croatia introduced an instant payment service in October 2020 for transactions in kuna up to a certain limit [oai_citation:37‡data.ecb.europa.eu]. This system (NKSInst) enabled bank customers to send and receive money within seconds at any time, providing immediate clearing. With Eurozone entry, an EuroNCSInst service was set up to handle instant euro transfers, aligned with the SEPA Instant Credit Transfer scheme. The instant payment platform operates continuously, with final settlement occurring via dedicated accounts at the central bank. Most Croatian banks quickly joined, making instant payments widely available. By design, it uses ISO 20022 messaging and mirrors European instant payment standards.

NKS was the deferred net settlement system for retail payments (paperless credits, direct debits, etc.) in Croatia’s domestic currency. Launched in 2001 [oai_citation:34‡data.ecb.europa.eu], it cleared high volumes of low-value transactions among banks, with multilateral net positions settled at day-end in the RTGS [oai_citation:35‡hnb.hr]. The service operated multiple clearing cycles per day for efficiency. In 2016, a EuroNCS was introduced in parallel to clear euro-denominated retail payments [oai_citation:36‡data.ecb.europa.eu] (aligning with SEPA standards). After Croatia joined the Eurozone (2023), EuroNCS became the primary retail ACH system, and the kuna NKS was phased out. The clearing system is governed by the CNB’s regulations and overseen by the National Payment System Committee.
Mobile wallet
Primary payment method

Owned and run by Banque de la République d’Haïti (BRH). SPIH settles credit transfers between commercial banks in real-time, supports monetary operations and high-value customer payments. It replaced manual clearing to increase safety and traceability.
EMTECH and HaitiPay demonstrated issuance, wallet distribution and offline transfers of a BRH-backed CBDC using DLT and API gateways in 2022.

NatCash is the mobile wallet offered by telecommunications company NATCOM S.A. (a Viettel-Haiti joint venture). Introduced in 2013 to boost digital finance, NatCash offers wallet-to-wallet transfers, merchant and bill payments (utility, mobile), and cash in/out through agents [oai_citation:30‡streetinsider.com]. It operates on a nationwide agent network of ~3,000 outlets for liquidity [oai_citation:31‡streetinsider.com]. NatCash transactions settle through Haiti’s interbank infrastructure (the net positions are cleared via the SPIH RTGS). Adoption has been growing, with NatCash promoting a secure payments ecosystem aimed at financial inclusion [oai_citation:32‡streetinsider.com]. While it trails MonCash in market share, it is considered one of Haiti’s key payment rails.
Established 2007, PRONAP routes debit/credit card transactions and ATM withdrawals among banks. It also links to mobile-money operators and supports domestic routing to reduce USD cash usage.

SPIH (Système de Paiement Interbancaire Haïtien) is Haiti’s Real-Time Gross Settlement system, operated by the Banque de la République d’Haiti (BRH). It was established as part of the 2007 PRONAP project to modernize payments [oai_citation:21‡afi-global.org]. SPIH settles high-value, time-critical transactions individually and irrevocably in real time. All licensed banks and the BRH participate, using SPIH for interbank transfers in HTG and foreign currency. The system enables immediate finality for wholesale payments (e.g. government payments, large corporate transfers). SPIH also acts as the settlement backbone for other payment instruments (cheques, cards, electronic transfers) in Haiti. Adoption is mandatory for all banks, but domestic usage is limited by low banking penetration. BRH oversight ensures security and compliance with international standards.

MonCash is Haiti’s largest mobile money service, operated by Digicel Haiti. Launched in 2011 as part of a financial inclusion drive, it enables P2P transfers, international remittances, bill payments, airtime top-up, and merchant payments [oai_citation:26‡moncashdfs.com]. Users register via Digicel network; accounts can hold HTG or USD. MonCash serves both the banked and unbanked population, leveraging Digicel’s extensive agent network for cash-in/cash-out. The service integrates with the banking system for funding and remittances. It has seen rapid growth: over 2 million users are registered [oai_citation:27‡moncashdfs.com]. MonCash processes hundreds of thousands of transactions monthly (specific figures unpublished) and is credited with expanding access to digital payments in Haiti.

The National Payments Processor (PRONAP) is Haiti’s central switching and clearing system, implemented by the central bank in 2007 [oai_citation:23‡afi-global.org]. PRONAP operates the national card and electronic clearing house (ACH), routing transactions among banks for cards, debit, credit, and electronic transfers. Through PRONAP, Visa/MasterCard (introduced 1996) and local card schemes (e.g. in-country debit) comply with international standards [oai_citation:24‡afi-global.org]. The switch enabled online processing of domestic payments that were previously offline. Though comprehensive usage is limited, PRONAP underpins clearing of retail payments and is being adapted to support mobile money integration. It is regulated by BRH but operated in partnership with banks.
National payment system
Online payments

Hungary’s domestic instant payment service (RBIPS) was launched on 1 July 2019. Developed by GIRO in partnership with Nets, it enables end-users to send real-time credit transfers up to HUF10 million around-the-clock [oai_citation:63‡fintechfutures.com]. The payer can use the beneficiary’s mobile number instead of account details. Inter-bank settlement occurs immediately, with finality similar to cash. Banks were mandated by law to offer this service as a basic feature for customers. The infrastructure is integrated with the ICS instant leg (since 2020). IPS transactions are processed via the clearing system (settling via MNB’s prefunded accounts), with liquidity provided by MNB if needed during off-RTGS hours. The system has dramatically increased the use of digital payments. Adoption is universal (all banks must participate by regulation), and volumes have surged. The service also supports QR-code payments and request-to-pay functions. MNB’s oversight ensures broad accessibility and resilience [oai_citation:64‡fintechfutures.com].

Hungary, while not in the Eurozone, participates in SEPA clearing for euro transactions. Euro credit transfers (SCT) and direct debits (SDD) initiated in Hungary are handled by EU Automated Clearing Houses. GIRO’s systems interface with SWIFT-based SEPA clearing and settlement (via EBA Clearing etc.) [oai_citation:66‡giro.hu]. The domestic ICS does not directly clear SEPA payments, but Hungarian banks join Euro payments through certified ACHs. This ensures cross-border euro transfers are processed in line with EU standards. The Hungarian Banking Association coordinated SEPA implementation. VIBER and ICS serve HUF; SEPA transfers flow through external EU infrastructure.

Card payments in Hungary are processed through several clearing systems. International card networks (Visa, Mastercard) dominate consumer card transactions. GIRO/ICS handles interbank settlement of domestic debit cards via Girocard and domestic payment schemes. Retailers’ POS terminals connect through acquiring banks to card networks. On the issuing side, the GIRO clearing house settles net positions between banks overnight or intraday. Contactless EMV and mobile wallets (Apple Pay, GPay) overlay these networks. Hungary also had domestic card initiatives (e.g. MOL Pay, OTPay), but none have overtaken Visa/MC. The National Bank oversees card systems; net settlement balances are ultimately cleared via RTGS (VIBER) or ACH. Adoption of cards is high in urban areas, but cash still significant in rural regions.

VIBER is the Real-Time Gross Settlement system operated by Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB). It has been in operation since 3 September 1999 [oai_citation:54‡mnb.hu]. VIBER settles large-value interbank HUF and government transactions individually, immediately and irrevocably. Participants include all credit institutions, the state treasury, central bank and the post office [oai_citation:55‡mnb.hu]. The system runs daily from 07:00 to 18:00. VIBER uses SWIFT messaging for instructions, and supports banks’ liquidity management (with intraday credit against collateral, queuing, priorities) [oai_citation:56‡mnb.hu]. It is MNB’s designated system for high-value settlement and key for monetary policy operations. Typical uses include interbank transfers, FX trades settlement, central bank operations, and DvP settlement. Volumes are very high (billions of HUF per day), reflecting virtually all large funds movements in Hungary.
Operated by Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB) since 1999; processes inter-bank and central-bank operations with daylight credit and SWIFT access.

The ICS, run by GIRO Elszámolásforgalmi Zrt., is Hungary’s centralized clearing house for retail payments. It processes high-volume, low-value transactions: credit transfers and direct debits between banks. The system operates on multiple rails: an overnight batch, intraday clearing, and since 2 March 2020 an instant clearing service for customer transfers [oai_citation:58‡mnb.hu]. ICS is the backbone of domestic retail payments and classified by MNB as an “important payment system.” Transactions submitted by banks are netted and settled, with net positions cleared via MNB (accounting with VIBER). Since 2019, Hungary has an instant payment overlay: virtually any ICS participant can submit a single credit transfer that is settled in seconds 24/7 (via ICS instant settlement) [oai_citation:59‡fintechfutures.com]. Together ICS and its instant legs handle billions of transactions annually [oai_citation:60‡giro.hu], reflecting near-universal bank transfer use. It ensures rapid interbank clearing, supports payment innovation (QR codes, e-wallets integration) and continuous availability. The ICS also coordinates SEPA clearing (SCT and SDD) through SEPA ACHs, though direct GIRO clearing is used predominantly for forint transactions.
Launched March 2020; all Hungarian PSPs must route qualifying credit transfers through AFR. Includes secondary identifiers and request-to-pay; will support QR/NFC ‘qvik’ standard from 2025.

sistemas.nome: AFR (Azonnali Fizetési Rendszer / Instant Payment System)

sistemas.descricao: Bank Indonesia-operated infrastructure for 24/7 instant fund transfers using mobile numbers or virtual IDs. Processes transactions in under 22 seconds with tiered fees (IDR 2,500-7,500). Integrated with mobile banking apps and e-wallets. Supports bulk disbursements and inbound cross-border payments .
Comprehensive payment system governance framework
sistemas.detalhes: Replaced BI Regulation 18/2016, establishing principles for payment stability, security, and inclusion. Covers licensing, Rupiah management, and digital currency oversight. Mandates interoperability between banks and fintechs, with sanctions for non-compliance including license revocation. Aligns with international standards like PCI-DSS and ISO 20022 .

sistemas.descricao: Wholesale CBDC pilot
Dominant e-wallets integrated with super apps
National QR code payment standard
Central backbone since 2000; Gen II launched 2015; settles >95 % of interbank value, supports intraday repo liquidity.
Clears cheques, giro, credit transfers in nine cycles/day; per-tx cap IDR 1 B; fee IDR 3 500.

sistemas.nome: BI-RTGS (Bank Indonesia Real Time Gross Settlement)

sistemas.descricao: Euro payment standard
Neobank adoption
Irish PSPs clear bulk SEPA credit transfers via STEP2 and CORE, while few BICs currently reachable for SCT Inst (6 % in 2023). Regulation 2024/886 will mandate instant reachability by 2025.
Central Bank of Ireland operates national component; processes high-value payments, monetary operations and SEPA settlement; migrated to ISO 20022 in March 2023.
National payment app
Card processing

ZAHAV enables immediate and irrevocable settlement of high-value interbank payments. Operated by the Bank of Israel since 2007, it provides final settlement on a per-transaction basis. Participants include all Israeli banks and primary dealers. Payments are settled via BOI accounts, ensuring finality in real time.

This instant payment system, operated by the Bank Settlement Center (Masav), enables real-time credit transfers between participating banks. Payments arrive in the beneficiary’s account within 5–7 seconds and are final on receipt [oai_citation:4‡boi.org.il]. Launched in the early 2020s, it allows consumers and businesses to send small-value payments (e.g. person-to-person, bill payments) instantly without using cash.

KNET is a consortium-owned payments network established in 1992 [oai_citation:9‡cbk.gov.kw]. It interconnects ATMs, POS terminals and mobile channels of Israeli banks, enabling interoperable cash withdrawals and card payments across institutions. All commercial banks participate, providing widespread ATM access and card services (debit/credit) to consumers.

ASHRAIT is SHVA’s proprietary card-acquiring clearing system that processes domestic and international credit/debit card transactions [oai_citation:6‡shva.co.il]. It supports EMV chip cards and maintains settlement between issuing and acquiring banks. The system handles authorization, clearing and settlement for card payments at ATMs and POS terminals, generating confirmations and performing fraud checks [oai_citation:7‡shva.co.il].

UPI is India’s instant mobile fund transfer system operated by NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India). Launched in 2016, it allows individuals to send and receive money from their bank accounts using a smartphone, 24/7, using simple identifiers like mobile numbers or UPI IDs. Transactions (P2P, P2M) are processed in real time. Banks and third-party apps (PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm, etc.) serve as UPI frontend providers. UPI has seen explosive adoption: it handled ~185.9 billion transactions in FY2024–25 [oai_citation:74‡medianama.com], accounting for ~84% of retail digital payments. The system scales to billions per month [oai_citation:75‡bis.org]. It supports merchant payments, bill pays, QR-code payments, and even international corridors. NPCI ensures interoperability, security, and low fees. UPI transfers are settled through NPCI’s clearing to bank accounts via RBI (RTGS/NEFT) rail. Adoption is extremely high (almost universal among smartphone users) due to low barriers and government push.
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) under RBI regulation, UPI enables real-time payments 24/7 using virtual payment addresses or QR codes. It processes transactions through a centralized switch with immediate settlement, supporting both bank account transfers and mobile wallet integrations. The system uses a layered architecture with NPCI as the central switch facilitating interoperability between participating banks and payment service providers. UPI supports features like collect request (payee-initiated payments), recurring payments, and international cross-border linkages .

sistemas.descricao: High-value real-time settlement system for large transactions
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by Reserve Bank of India (RBI), RTGS processes individual transactions in real-time with final settlement in central bank money. It handles high-value transactions (minimum ₹2 lakh) with no upper limit, operating 24/7/365. Transactions settle individually on gross basis with payments being final and irrevocable once processed. The system is primarily used for interbank transfers, large corporate payments, and securities settlements. RBI provides a positive confirmation system where remitters receive notification when funds reach beneficiary accounts .

sistemas.descricao: Batched electronic funds transfer system for all value transactions
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by RBI, NEFT processes electronic transfers in half-hourly batches 24/7. Unlike RTGS, it has no minimum amount requirement and settles transactions on a deferred net settlement basis. Funds typically reach beneficiaries within two hours of batch processing. NEFT supports both individual and bulk transactions, with return mechanisms for failed credits within two hours of processing. The system is integrated with all major banks and widely used for salary payments, vendor settlements, and retail remittances .

sistemas.descricao: Domestic card payment scheme with global acceptance
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by NPCI, RuPay is India's indigenous card network competing with Visa/Mastercard. It offers debit, credit, and prepaid cards with features including contactless payments, offline wallet functionality for transit, and international acceptance. The network uses NPCI SecureNxt for 3D-secure authentication and supports tokenization for secure digital payments. RuPay cards comply with National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) specifications for transit payments across metros and buses. The system operates on a not-for-profit model, keeping processing costs low for banks .

sistemas.descricao: Bulk payment system for high-volume repetitive transactions
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by NPCI, NACH processes high-volume, recurring payments like subsidies, salaries, dividends, loan EMI collections, and utility bill payments. It consolidates regional ECS systems into a national platform with standardized rules. Key components include the Aadhaar Payment Bridge for Direct Benefit Transfers using Aadhaar numbers, Mandate Management System for authorization controls, and Dispute Management System. NACH processes files in batches with next-day settlement cycles through RBI's clearing mechanism .

sistemas.descricao: IMPS, launched in 2010 by NPCI, is India’s first 24x7 instant interbank electronic payment service. It allows account holders to send money instantly using mobile banking, ATM or online banking via MMID or mobile number. IMPS handles transactions up to a daily limit (set by RBI); currently customers can transfer up to ₹2 lakh in a single IMPS transaction. While UPI has largely overtaken consumer usage, IMPS remains in use especially for corporate bulk transfers and in systems that predate UPI. NPCI continues to support IMPS infrastructure. Adoption is high (all banks participate), but volumes are now smaller compared to UPI. Nonetheless, IMPS pioneered round-the-clock P2P transfers and is integrated into many banking apps and schemes.
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by NPCI, IMPS enables instant interbank transfers through multiple channels (mobile, internet, ATM) using MMID (Mobile Money Identifier) or IFSC. It processes transactions in real-time with immediate beneficiary credit, operating as a layered system atop existing NEFT infrastructure. IMPS supports features like request-pull transactions and is integrated with UPI for backward compatibility. Transaction limits are typically lower than RTGS but available 24/7 including holidays .

sistemas.descricao: Mobile-based payment apps with integrated financial services
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by private entities (e.g., Paytm, PhonePe, Google Pay) under RBI's Prepaid Payment Instrument (PPI) guidelines. These wallets store value digitally and enable P2P transfers, merchant payments, bill payments, and transit fares. They integrate with UPI for bank transfers and support features like bill splitting, investments, and mini-app ecosystems. RBI mandates full KYC compliance for full-function wallets and regulates interoperability between wallet providers .

sistemas.descricao: Biometric-based payment system for financial inclusion
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by NPCI, AEPS enables bank transactions using Aadhaar authentication at micro-ATMs. It supports basic services like cash withdrawal, deposit, balance inquiry, and Aadhaar-to-Aadhaar funds transfer through Business Correspondents. Transactions are authorized via biometric verification linked to Aadhaar, requiring no physical cards or phones. Primarily used in rural areas and for Direct Benefit Transfer subsidies under government schemes .

sistemas.descricao: Digital sovereign currency pilot for retail and wholesale
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by RBI under the Payments Vision 2025, the e₹ is a digital token legal tender equivalent to physical currency. The retail version (CBDC-R) uses distributed ledger technology for P2P and P2M transactions via digital wallets, while the wholesale version (CBDC-W) facilitates interbank settlement. Current pilots test programmable features for government welfare transfers and offline functionality. Cross-border use cases are being explored through multilateral CBDC bridges .

sistemas.descricao: Financial inclusion programs leveraging payment infrastructure
sistemas.detalhes: Government-led initiatives using NPCI/RBI payment rails: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) provides zero-balance accounts with RuPay cards; Kisan Credit Card (KCC) offers agricultural credit via RuPay cards; National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) enables interoperable transit payments. These integrate with Aadhaar and mobile numbers for direct benefit transfers, leveraging the Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile (JAM) trinity. Budget 2025 expanded KCC limits to ₹5 lakh and introduced custom credit cards for micro-enterprises .

sistemas.descricao: Emerging crypto-based payment channels in regulatory gray area
sistemas.detalhes: Unregulated crypto payment channels operating in legal ambiguity. Despite Supreme Court overturning RBI's 2018 ban, the 'Banning of Cryptocurrency & Regulation of Official Digital Currency Bill 2019' remains pending. Some exchanges facilitate crypto-to-UPI payments via P2P arrangements, though RBI discourages banking relationships with crypto entities. Transactions occur on blockchain networks with volatility and settlement risks .

sistemas.descricao: International payment integrations with UPI
sistemas.detalhes: UPI's expansion to enable cross-border remittances through bilateral linkages: UPI-PayNow (Singapore) allows real-time transfers using virtual payment addresses; discussions ongoing with EU's TIPS, Japan, and UAE. Operated by NPCI with partner central banks, these use near-real-time forex conversion and comply with FEMA regulations. RBI is exploring settling foreign currencies on Indian systems through bilateral arrangements .

sistemas.descricao: NACH is NPCI’s automated clearing house, introduced in 2010 (replacing ECS). It facilitates bulk, periodic payments (both credit and debit) such as payroll, pension, dividends, utility bills, loan EMIs and recurring mandates. Banks submit files of payment instructions (e.g. salary payroll or standing debits) to NPCI, which nets and processes them overnight. Settlement occurs through the RBI – either via RTGS or through bank liquidity. NACH has standardized and greatly expanded bulk payments in India. Nearly all major recurring payment streams (e.g. employee salaries, government subsidies) flow through NACH. Its adoption is very high for corporate and institutional payments. (NACH transactions volume is in the billions per year, although exact latest figures are not publicly reported.)

sistemas.nome: National Automated Clearing House – High Value (NACH-HV)
sistemas.descricao: A variant of NACH, the NACH-HV (formerly NACH-RTGS) provides near-real-time funds transfer for high-value transactions between banks for selected government and institutional payments (like tax refunds, major vendor payments). It was introduced to reduce time taken for high-value bulk payments. NACH-HV uses the existing RTGS infrastructure for net settlement, delivering credits in under an hour. Its adoption is growing for designated high-value disbursements, although UPI and RTGS handle most urgent transfers.

India’s RTGS is operated by the Reserve Bank of India and processes high-value interbank transfers in real time (final settlement individually). It handles transactions of any amount (no minimum limit) after Dec 2020 when RTGS was made 24x7 [oai_citation:77‡medianama.com]. RTGS is used for large corporate, interbank, and government payments. As per RBI (Mar 2025), RTGS is available across 173,000 bank branches [oai_citation:78‡medianama.com]. In FY2024–25, RTGS saw a ~12% volume increase [oai_citation:79‡angelone.in]. All commercial banks must participate. RTGS operates continuously, and it also settles net positions from other systems (e.g., NEFT, ACH/NACH). It uses banks’ accounts at RBI for settlement. The system supports priority queuing and liquidity management. Iconically, RTGS handles funds much like cash-equivalent settlement in the banking system.

NEFT is India’s nationwide batch fund transfer system operated by RBI. Introduced in 2005, it allows one-way transfers to beneficiary bank accounts using IFSC codes. NEFT operates in half-hourly batches around the clock (24x7) since Dec 2019. There is no minimum or maximum limit per transaction (subject to individual banks’ internal ceilings) [oai_citation:81‡rbi.org.in]. NEFT supports all retail and corporate payments like salary, utility bills, loan repayments, education fees, and inward/outward remittances (e.g. to Nepal). As of Mar 2025, NEFT is available at 174,000+ branches [oai_citation:82‡medianama.com]. NEFT instructions submitted by banks are netted and settled via RBI’s accounts (via RTGS). Millions of transactions are processed each day. Adoption is very high across India due to ubiquity (almost all banks offer NEFT) and government mandates. NEFT greatly reduced cheque usage and expanded digital payment penetration in India.

BBPS is a centralized payment platform for retail payments like electricity, water, gas, telecom, DTH and other utility bills. Launched in 2017 by NPCI, it connects billers, banks and non-bank Bharat Bill Payment Operating Units (BBPOUs). Consumers can pay any participating bill through multiple channels (bank branches, ATMs, internet banking, mobile apps, BBPS agents) with instant confirmation. BBPS aggregates bill presentment and payment clearance. Funds are collected centrally and remitted to billers within one or two days via NEFT/RTGS clearing. By improving ease and interoperability, BBPS has seen rapid adoption nationwide. It handles hundreds of millions of bill payments annually.

CTS is the process of cheque clearing where a digital image of the cheque is transmitted for clearing instead of the physical cheque. India adopted cheque truncation nationwide to speed up cheque clearance and reduce courier costs. All bank branches participate via regional clearing houses. Truncated images and electronic data are exchanged between banks, and settlement occurs through NEFT/RTGS. Cheque clearing now mostly settles within one day. CTS is operated by RBI oversight through Cheque Truncation Centres. Adoption is universal for cheque instruments, though cheque volumes have fallen steeply in favor of electronic methods.

RuPay is India’s indigenous card payment scheme, developed by NPCI. It provides domestic Visa/Mastercard-equivalent debit and credit cards to member banks. RuPay cards work at POS, ATMs and e-commerce with acceptance growing rapidly. Initially low-profile, RuPay has expanded through government promotion (e.g. Jan Dhan accounts) and card on UPI. By 2023, RuPay cards numbered hundreds of millions and made tens of billions of transactions. Settlements for RuPay transactions are cleared through NPCI’s clearing to banks (via RTGS/NEFT). RuPay operates alongside international networks, offering lower merchant fees. Adoption has become very high, especially in debit card space (NPCI claims RuPay dominates debit card volumes).
RBI-owned system clearing retail credit transfers; supports API and branch initiation; no amount ceiling.
Operated by Reserve Bank of India (RBI); 24×7 since Dec 2020; minimum INR 200,000, ISO 20022 XML messages via SFMS.
NPCI-operated switch providing real-time credit in <15 s; backbone for UPI; addresses via MMID or account+IFSC.
Built on IMPS rails by NPCI (2016). Supports VPA aliases, request-to-pay, QR, recurring e-mandates and credit lines. Free for consumers; 15 Bn tx/month Nov 2024.

MBK-RTGS is the Central Bank of Iceland’s real-time gross settlement system for large-value payments. It settles high-value interbank transfers (typically ≥10 million ISK) in real time on a gross basis [oai_citation:68‡cb.is]. This on-ledger system ensures immediate finality. MBK-RTGS operates during banking hours (with a later cutoff for customer transactions) and supports liquidity management with intraday collateralized credit. Participants include all commercial banks, the Icelandic treasury, and securities depositories. The central bank regulates and operates MBK-RTGS under legal rules (2020 regulations) [oai_citation:69‡cb.is]. Large corporate, government, and interbank transactions (e.g. forex trades, central bank open market ops, securities DvP legs) use MBK-RTGS.
Middleware that receives payment messages from banks, analyses amount and routes to MBK-RTGS or EXP; performs format translation and sanctions screening.

Aur is a pilot project by Icelandic banks (e.g. Íslandsbanki, Landsbanki) and MNB, designing a central bank-backed digital currency/settlement token. It is a private DLT platform where banks issue tokenized deposits and securities, enabling real-time DvP settlement. Currently in a testing phase, Aur simulates issuance of a wholesale CBDC to enable instant settlement of interbank FX and bond trades. It is not open to the public. So far it has completed proof-of-concept stages. Adoption: pilot (planned rollout if successful). It's noted by financial authorities as a research innovation for future finance. (No live volumes; demonstration only).
Launched 2020 as part of the MBK upgrade (RTGS, EXP, PAYHUB). Handles ISK <10 M transfers via bank channels; settlement netted twice daily in MBK-RTGS.
Part of the interbank payment system operated by Seðlabanki Íslands; settles large-value payments and securities cash legs six times daily.

MBK-Inst is Iceland’s continuous retail payment platform, introduced by the Central Bank. It processes low-value electronic transfers (typically under 10 million ISK) between banks and their customers. The system operates 24/7 for transaction initiation [oai_citation:71‡cb.is], but clears payments in two daily settlement runs (at 08:30 and 16:00). Banks transfer net positions from MBK-Inst into MBK-RTGS for final settlement [oai_citation:72‡cb.is]. This structure provides real-time acceptance and finality within hours. All licensed Icelandic banks participate. MBK-Inst greatly speeds up day-to-day retail and business payments compared to the previous one-day clearing cycle. It is essential for payments between individuals and businesses (salary transfers, invoices, P2P), dramatically reducing cash usage. Central Bank oversight ensures system reliability and integration with MBK-RTGS.

Kortasamband (formerly Korta) is the national organization managing card and ATM networks in Iceland. It provides clearing and settlement for domestic debit and credit card transactions and ATM withdrawals. All Icelandic banks participate, and their cards (e.g. Visa EMV co-badged) are cleared through this switch. Kortasamband ensures authorizations, clearing and net settlement of POS and ATM transactions among member banks. It also interfaces with international card networks for cross-border payments. The system settles via the banks’ accounts at the Central Bank (RTGS) at end of day. While cash is still used, card usage is high in Iceland (virtually all point-of-sale terminals accept cards). Kortasamband also supports mobile wallets integrated with card credentials.

GEPA is a centralized treasury and payment platform for government salaries, pensions and public sector payments. Operated by the Bank of Italy in collaboration with the Ministry of Finance, it consolidates government accounts under a unified treasury account system (starting 2009) [oai_citation:13‡bancaditalia.it]. GEPA handles high-value salary disbursements and channels funds through standard payment networks (RTGS, ACH).

Bancomat is the domestic ATM network allowing cash withdrawals and balance inquiries across Italian banks [oai_citation:15‡en.wikipedia.org]#:~:text=Bancomat%20is%20an%20Italian%20interbank,for%20use%20with%20%2045). It is owned by Bancomat S.p.A. and connects over 53,000 ATMs. Cards issued by Italian banks carry the Bancomat logo for ATM access nationwide.

PagoBANCOMAT is the interbank network for debit card transactions in Italy [oai_citation:17‡en.wikipedia.org]#:~:text=In%201986%2C%20an%20associated%20debit,based%20%2048%20transactions). It allows PIN-based purchases at POS terminals nationwide. It is owned by Bancomat S.p.A. and all major banks participate. Most Bancomat/PagoBANCOMAT cards are co-badged with international schemes (e.g. Maestro) for global use.

Bancomat Pay is a mobile payment app provided by Bancomat S.p.A., enabling smartphone users to pay via QR codes and transfers. It links to a customer's bank account and supports immediate online payments for merchants and P2P transfers [oai_citation:19‡en.wikipedia.org]#:~:text=A%20new%20service%20called%20Bancomat,3).

Satispay is a smartphone-based payment app allowing peer-to-peer transfers and in-store payments in Italy [oai_citation:21‡pymnts.com]. Users link bank accounts to the app. Transactions use QR codes or phone numbers and are processed through Satispay’s proprietary infrastructure.

PagoPA is a government-managed electronic payments infrastructure that enables individuals and businesses to pay public administration fees, taxes and utilities. Payments are initiated via banks or PSPs through the PagoPA portal using a standardized payment reference (IUV) [oai_citation:23‡n26.com].
Mobile wallet

JamClear RTGS processes large-value (≥J$1M) and time-critical interbank transfers in real time [oai_citation:29‡boj.org.jm]. Operated by BOJ, it settles transactions immediately using central bank accounts, ensuring finality. Participants include all deposit-taking banks, primary dealers, and government entities.

The ACH, operated by Automated Payments Ltd (APL) and executed by J.E.T.S. Ltd., clears cheques, credits and debits on a net settlement basis [oai_citation:33‡boj.org.jm]. Items that exceed RTGS limits use the ACH; most salaries, recurring payments and retail transfers settle in night-time clearing cycles.

JamClear CSD is Jamaica’s securities depository system (introduced 2009) which records and settles government and BOJ securities. It automatically settles cash legs of securities trades via BOJ-RTGS [oai_citation:31‡boj.org.jm]. It facilitates government bond auctions, secondary market trades and corporate actions for domestic securities.

MultiLink is Jamaica’s interbank ATM/POS network (launched 1997) [oai_citation:35‡boj.org.jm]. It allows customers of member banks to withdraw cash and make purchases across banks. It is operated by a consortium of banks and financial institutions.
Quality Network (QNet) serves Jamaica’s credit unions. It provides ATM and debit card services (JCCUL Easi Access) and back-office processing to member credit unions [oai_citation:37‡boj.org.jm].

RTGS-JO, operated by the Central Bank of Jordan since 2002, settles large-value and interbank payments individually in real time [oai_citation:43‡cbj.gov.jo]. It also nets the clearing positions of retail systems, including JoMoPay and others. The system uses ISO 20022 messaging over SWIFT for final settlement.

JoMoPay is Jordan’s real-time retail payment platform for low-value transfers. Operated by the CBJ, it interconnects banks and telecoms, enabling mobile wallet transactions, bill payments and P2P transfers. Net positions are settled via RTGS-JO [oai_citation:45‡cbj.gov.jo]. Launched in 2014, it runs 24/7 to include unbanked segments.

BOJ-NET is Japan’s real-time gross settlement system for funds and government securities. It handles large interbank transfers, foreign exchange, and the delivery-versus-payment settlement of JGBs [oai_citation:39‡boj.or.jp]. All domestic banks participate via accounts at the BOJ; transfers are final and irrevocable upon settlement.

The Zengin System, operated by the Japanese Banks’ Payment Clearing Network, relays and nets retail credit transfers (e.g. wage payments, bill payments). Data is forwarded in real time to recipient banks, while net clearing positions are sent at end-of-day to the BOJ for settlement [oai_citation:41‡zengin-net.jp]. The 7th-generation Zengin handles nearly all interbank retail transactions in Japan.

PesaLink, operated by the Kenya Bankers Association, is an instant payment platform launched in 2014. It allows bank customers to send and receive money 24/7 using mobile or internet banking via an alias (phone number or email). Payments settle instantly between accounts, with central bank clearing.

KEPSS (Kenya Electronic Payment and Settlement System) is an RTGS used for high-value interbank transfers [oai_citation:51‡centralbank.go.ke]. Operated by CBK, it settles transactions individually in real time using central bank accounts, mitigating settlement risk.

M-Pesa is the leading mobile money service in Kenya, enabling P2P transfers and payments via SIM cards and apps. Users top up with cash at agents and can pay merchants or send money to other M-Pesa or bank accounts. It handles billions of transactions per year, significantly boosting financial inclusion.

sistemas.descricao: Operated by NBKR, the SPK is a deferred-net settlement system for small and routine payments (e.g. payroll, bills, merchant transfers) [oai_citation:4‡nbkr.kg]. Transactions are aggregated and settled in batch, typically daily.

A nationwide QR code standard launched in May 2022, allowing customers to make bank-to-bank transfers by scanning a QR code [oai_citation:9‡8b.world]. It enables instant mobile payments across participating banks without needing account numbers.

Known as “Elcard” (sometimes “Elkart”), this is the national payment system for bank-issued cards. It connects all banks’ ATMs and POS terminals in the country, enabling cashless card payments. It is operated by the Interbank Processing Center under NBKR oversight [oai_citation:7‡nbkr.kg].

Run by the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic (NBKR), the RTGS (GSRPS) settles payments in real time, currency-by-currency. It is used for large-value or urgent transfers between banks [oai_citation:1‡nbkr.kg]. Each transaction is settled individually and immediately.

ELQR is Kyrgyzstan's national QR code payment system launched in May 2022. It enables users to send money from their online banking applications directly to any other bank or payment system within the country by scanning QR codes. The system processes over 67,000 QR codes nationwide and has recorded over 121 million transactions worth 182.4 billion soms. ELQR operates 24/7 and supports instant payments between different banks and payment providers.

Elkart is Kyrgyzstan's national payment card system designed to provide affordable, reliable banking services including non-cash payments, salary/pension receipts, and budget payments. The system includes chip cards for enhanced security and supports both contactless and traditional card transactions. Elkart cards are issued by multiple banks and accepted across the country's ATM and POS networks.

sistemas.descricao: Bakong is a next-generation payments platform launched by NBC in 2020, effectively a central bank digital currency (CBDC)-like system [oai_citation:102‡weforum.org]. It allows instant fund transfers in Cambodian riel or US dollars between participating banks, MFIs, and e-wallets on a shared ledger. Bakong uses distributed ledger technology (developed with Soramitsu) but is centrally managed by NBC [oai_citation:103‡weforum.org]. Users can transact via a mobile app or their bank’s app by scanning QR codes or selecting contacts. By mid-2023, Bakong had 70 member institutions and was being used for cross-border remittances (e.g., to Malaysia) [oai_citation:104‡opendevelopmentcambodia.net]. It aims to promote financial inclusion and reduce cash reliance.
sistemas.detalhes: Bakong is a digital payment infrastructure launched by the National Bank of Cambodia in 2020. It is a distributed-ledger (blockchain) system that facilitates instant retail payments in both Cambodian riel (KHR) and US dollars. Commercial banks, MFIs, and e-wallets connect to Bakong, allowing their customers to transact with each other instantly through a Bakong mobile app or integrated services (https://www.kapronasia.com/asia-payments-research-category/cambodia-s-bakong-goes-from-strength-to-strength.html#:~:text=The%20volume%20of%20transactions%20in,on%20Bakong%20during%202024). Users can scan QR codes or select contacts to pay, and funds are moved across institutions on the Bakong ledger within seconds. It effectively serves as a quasi-CBDC (though technically claims to be a centralized DLT system) promoting dollar-riel interoperability. Type: 24/7 instant retail system (DLT-based). Operated by NBC.

sistemas.descricao: Mobile wallet
Interbank electronic funds transfer system for same-day retail payments
sistemas.detalhes: FAST is an interbank payment switch introduced by NBC in 2016 to enable quick (near real-time) low-value transfers among banks. It links the core banking systems of participating banks so that a customer can send money to another bank’s customer typically within minutes during operating hours. Initially capped at KHR 40 million per transaction, FAST provided a bridge between traditional ACH (next-day) and instant needs. It uses centralized clearing at NBC throughout the day. With Bakong’s advent, FAST now primarily backs up or handles non-Bakong participants. Type: Rapid retail transfer system (quasi-instant). Operated by NBC.

sistemas.descricao: Leading private mobile payment services integrated with Bakong
sistemas.detalhes: Before and alongside Bakong, Cambodia developed a vibrant private e-payment sector. ACLEDA Unity (by ACLEDA Bank) and Wing Money (a prominent MFS provider) are two major platforms. Wing, launched 2009, provides a nationwide agent-based money transfer and bill payment service. ACLEDA Unity allows bank customers to use phone banking for transfers and merchant payments. These services now connect to Bakong for interoperability – e.g., Wing joined Bakong, enabling its users to transact with banking system wallets. They still maintain proprietary networks of agents and merchant acceptance. Type: Mobile wallet/payment services (private).

sistemas.descricao: Launched in July 2023, the Cambodian Shared Switch is an NBC-operated network that connects banks’ ATMs and POS terminals for domestic card transactions [oai_citation:107‡khmertimeskh.com]. Prior to CSS, card interoperability was limited, with some bilateral arrangements. Now, any member bank’s debit card can be used to withdraw or pay at any other member’s ATM/POS, greatly expanding convenience [oai_citation:108‡vattanacbank.com]. CSS also provides a local card scheme option to reduce dependency on international networks for domestic payments. As of launch, major banks have joined, and the system is expected to lower costs for local card usage. CSS transactions are cleared through NBC (likely via the upcoming retail payments switch).
sistemas.detalhes: The CSS is an interbank card switch launched by NBC to connect ATM and POS networks of different banks. It ensures that ATM cardholders of one bank can withdraw at another bank’s ATM domestically. It also enables local routing of Mastercard/Visa transactions in local currency. Cambodia’s banking association and NBC promote CSS to reduce dependence on international networks and lower fees. All major banks are members, and ATM/POS devices are gradually linked to CSS. Type: Card switch & clearing. Operator: NBC in cooperation with Bakong team.

sistemas.descricao: FAST is an interbank payment system introduced by NBC in 2016 as a precursor to Bakong [oai_citation:106‡bakong.nbc.gov.kh]. It allowed quick account-to-account money transfers between banks on the same day, improving on traditional next-day clearing. Customers could initiate FAST transfers via online banking or mobile banking, and funds would be available within minutes if during operating hours. While basic (it functioned like an ACH with frequent cycles), FAST was pivotal in shifting Cambodia towards electronic payments. With Bakong’s introduction, FAST has been largely subsumed or integrated into the Bakong infrastructure, but it laid the groundwork for instant payments.
Cash-dominated economy with regulated mobile money.

Integrated Automated Transfer System under development for Comoros
sistemas.detalhes: The Union of Comoros, a small island economy, is in the process of modernizing its national payment infrastructure with an Automated Transfer System (ATS) that will combine RTGS for high-value payments and an ACH for retail bulk payments (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/812791592801563444/pdf/Comoros-Payments-and-Settlement-Systems-Oversight-Policy-Framework.pdf#:~:text=,will%20also%20absorb%20the) (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/812791592801563444/pdf/Comoros-Payments-and-Settlement-Systems-Oversight-Policy-Framework.pdf#:~:text=One%20of%20the%20statutory%20objectives,will%20also%20absorb%20the). Implemented with support from development partners (World Bank/AfDB), this new system will replace largely manual processes. The RTGS module will allow real-time settlement of large or urgent transfers in Comorian franc (KMF) among the few banks, the Treasury, and the central bank (BCC), greatly reducing settlement risk. The ACH module will automate the clearing of cheques and low-value electronic transfers, which until recently were exchanged physically at the central bank’s clearing house (https://banque-comores.km/r/systeme-de-paiement#:~:text=%C3%A0%20ordre%2C%20le%20virement%20et,Jeudi%2019%20Janvier%202023) (https://banque-comores.km/r/systeme-de-paiement#:~:text=chambre%20de%20compensation%20Face%20au,compensation%20est%20un%20syst%C3%A8me%20interbancaire). Adoption is currently Pilot/Initial: as of 2024, the ATS is being rolled out, so banks are testing connections. Once live, adoption should become High, as it will be the only national platform for interbank payments. Transaction volumes in Comoros are relatively low – possibly a few thousand interbank payments per day – but the ATS will significantly improve efficiency and availability (introducing same-day or instant processing instead of multi-day delays). It also paves the way for digital channels like online banking and mobile money to integrate. In summary, Comoros’ ATS is a critical upgrade from rudimentary systems to a modern electronic payment hub covering both RTGS and ACH functions, currently in the process of implementation.

sistemas.descricao: Legacy cheque clearing house operated by BCC
sistemas.detalhes: Prior to the new ATS, Comoros has relied on a physical cheque clearing house ("Chambre de Compensation") at the central bank. As cheques and other paper instruments (like bills of exchange) are used, especially by government and businesses, banks meet daily at the BCC to exchange these items and calculate net positions (https://banque-comores.km/r/systeme-de-paiement#:~:text=%C3%A0%20ordre%2C%20le%20virement%20et,Jeudi%2019%20Janvier%202023) (https://banque-comores.km/r/systeme-de-paiement#:~:text=l%27%C3%A9largissement%20rapide%20du%20secteur%20bancaire,Jeudi%2019%20Janvier%202023). This manual clearing system has been in place since 2006 in Moroni to cope with growing cheque use following banking sector expansion (https://banque-comores.km/r/systeme-de-paiement#:~:text=%C3%A0%20ordre%2C%20le%20virement%20et,Jeudi%2019%20Janvier%202023) (https://banque-comores.km/r/systeme-de-paiement#:~:text=l%27%C3%A9largissement%20rapide%20du%20secteur%20bancaire,Jeudi%2019%20Janvier%202023). Adoption has been Medium: the few commercial banks and postal financial service use it to clear cheques – still a notable means of payment for salaries, vendor payments, etc., given limited electronic alternatives. The volume is modest (perhaps on the order of tens of thousands of cheques annually). Settlement of net balances occurs via central bank accounts (previously next-day). The new ACH in the ATS will supersede this chamber, bringing automated exchange. Until full ATS adoption, the cheque clearing house remains operational. It has provided a basic interbank settlement function in a cash-dominated economy. As electronic transfers and mobile money grow, cheque usage is expected to decline, but currently it still plays a role for larger or formal transactions in Comoros.

sistemas.descricao: Participation in Southern African regional cross-border RTGS (for Comorian franc to rand payments)
sistemas.detalhes: Comoros joined the Southern African Development Community (SADC) in 2017 and thereby became part of SADC’s regional payment initiatives. One is the SADC-RTGS (formerly known as SIRESS) – a multicurrency RTGS based in South Africa that settles cross-border payments among SADC countries in a common platform (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/812791592801563444/pdf/Comoros-Payments-and-Settlement-Systems-Oversight-Policy-Framework.pdf#:~:text=System%20,application%20to%20join%20the%20organization) (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/812791592801563444/pdf/Comoros-Payments-and-Settlement-Systems-Oversight-Policy-Framework.pdf#:~:text=of%20Comoros%20is%20the%20newest,application%20to%20join%20the%20organization). Currently SADC-RTGS primarily uses South African rand as the settlement currency (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/812791592801563444/pdf/Comoros-Payments-and-Settlement-Systems-Oversight-Policy-Framework.pdf#:~:text=match%20at%20L586%205%20The,transactions%20are%20settled%20in%20Rands) (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/812791592801563444/pdf/Comoros-Payments-and-Settlement-Systems-Oversight-Policy-Framework.pdf#:~:text=5%20The%20South%20African%20Reserve,transactions%20are%20settled%20in%20Rands). Comorian banks have very limited regional transactions, but in principle, if a bank needed to transfer funds to, say, Tanzania or South Africa, it could use SADC-RTGS rather than correspondent banks. Adoption in Comoros is Low so far – as the newest SADC member, Comoros has been preparing to integrate but actual usage is minimal (few Comorian banks have direct access yet). Over time, if trade with SADC grows (e.g., imports from South Africa), SADC-RTGS could provide faster, cheaper settlement (same-day in rand). It may also support Comorian franc in future if multi-currency expansion occurs. For now, it’s more of a potential benefit. In summary, Comoros’ connection to SADC-RTGS is at an early stage and volumes are likely near zero currently. It remains a strategic option for cross-border payment efficiency once Comorian financial institutions fully onboard to the system.

sistemas.descricao: Cash dominance and nascent mobile money usage in Comoros
sistemas.detalhes: Comoros is largely a cash-based economy. The majority of daily transactions – from local market purchases to salaries in rural areas – are done in cash (Comorian franc), given the low banking penetration and limited acceptance of digital payments. Adoption of cash is Very High: even government payrolls are often cashed out, and many people operate outside formal financial channels. At the same time, mobile phone penetration is rising, and there have been initial steps toward mobile money. The state telecom (Comoros Telecom) and potentially private telcos have explored mobile wallet services, but these remain in early stages with Pilot-level adoption. For example, a service called "M-Voula" was reportedly trialed around 2019, but scale is very limited (only a few thousand users). With donor support, Comoros aims to leverage mobile money to improve financial inclusion and facilitate remittances from diaspora. However, as of 2024, mobile money usage is still Low – most remittances come through Western Union/MoneyGram cash pickup. Some microfinance institutions are introducing mobile payments in cooperation with telcos. Crypto usage is virtually non-existent in Comoros. In sum, cash reigns supreme in Comoros’ payment landscape, and while mobile money has potential, it is only beginning to be introduced. The hope is that with the new ATS enabling e-money settlement and rising mobile access, mobile wallets could gradually take root to complement cash in the future.

sistemas.descricao: M-Vola is a mobile money platform introduced by Telma (Telecom Malagasy) in Comoros through its local subsidiary (branded as Yé! or Yupee). Launched in the late 2010s, it allows Comorians to send and receive money domestically using simple mobile phone commands, without needing a bank account. Users can deposit cash at Telma agent outlets, then use their phone to transfer funds to another user, pay certain bills, or buy telecom services. Given Comoros’ scattered islands and relatively low banking access, M-Vola provides a convenient alternative for remittances and payments. Usage is growing as Telma expands coverage, though overall mobile money adoption is still in early stages in Comoros. The service is fully managed by the telecom operator and not yet interoperable with bank systems.

SYCOCO is the Comoros clearing system for interbank payments, primarily used for cheque clearing. It operates as a manual or semi-manual clearinghouse where banks exchange cheque instruments and settlement positions are calculated. SYCOCO is currently the only interbank payment mechanism in the country [oai_citation:74‡documents1.worldbank.org]. It processes on average around 5,000 cheques monthly, worth about KMF 19.7 billion (USD 49.4 million) [oai_citation:75‡documents1.worldbank.org]. Final settlement of these net positions is done via the Central Bank of Comoros. The system is paper-based and relatively slow (cheque settlements can take several days). Comoros is in the process of modernizing its payment infrastructure to eventually replace SYCOCO with an automated system.
Tourist payments
The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank RTGS is the region’s large-value payment system, settling EC dollar payments in real time:contentReference[oaicite:24]{index=24}.

DCash is the ECCB’s digital Eastern Caribbean dollar pilot. It launched in 2021 in four countries (including St. Kitts) for P2P and merchant payments:contentReference[oaicite:27]{index=27}. The pilot ended in Jan 2024 with limited volume:contentReference[oaicite:28]{index=28}.

4Cs (Caribbean Credit Card Corporation) is a consortium-owned switch that processes domestic Visa/MasterCard payments across the ECCU. It provides authorization and clearing for ATM and POS transactions involving cards issued in any member state, settling net positions across banks. It effectively links all islands for card transactions.
The Caribbean Credit Card Corporation (4Cs) handles merchant acquiring and card clearing for Visa and Mastercard in the ECCU:contentReference[oaicite:26]{index=26}.

DCash is the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank’s digital currency pilot (launched 2019) [oai_citation:31‡eccb-centralbank.org]. It is a tokenized version of the Eastern Caribbean dollar (EC$) issued by the ECCB. DCash is distributed through banks and fintechs and used by consumers for P2P and P2M payments via a smartphone app [oai_citation:32‡eccb-centralbank.org]. The pilot, covering St. Kitts among others, explores inclusion and efficiency benefits of CBDC.

The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB) operates a RTGS (Large-Value Payment System) that settles high-value interbank and government payments in XCD [oai_citation:29‡eccb-centralbank.org]. This system (shared by all ECCU members) provides real-time gross settlement via SWIFT messages, ensuring final settlement for large transfers within the currency union.

The Eastern Caribbean Automated Clearing House (ECACH) is a multilateral net settlement system established by ECCB and ECCU banks [oai_citation:30‡eccb-centralbank.org]. It handles retail payments: domestic cheques, direct debits and electronic credit transfers in XCD. Cheques are cleared using imaging (ANSI X9.100-187) and electronic transfers use NACHA-like files. Net obligations are settled via the RTGS.
Exclusive payment method

North Korea has several state-run cash-card schemes (e.g. Sili Card, Narae, Jonsong, Koryo, Songbong) mainly for use in Pyongyang and select areas. These cards (tied to local or foreign-currency accounts) allow limited electronic payments at merchants and for remittances:contentReference[oaicite:17]{index=17}:contentReference[oaicite:18]{index=18}.

All other transactions are settled through the central banking system (Bank of DPRK). Details are opaque, but payments are recorded in ledger systems within state banks. No transparent public payment rails are reported.
North Korea has limited electronic payment options...
Real-time gross settlement system for high-value interbank transfers
sistemas.detalhes: Operated by the Bank of Korea (BOK), this hybrid RTGS system processes large-value payments including securities settlements, interbank lending, and retail payment system net settlements. It combines real-time gross settlement with continuous bilateral and multilateral offsetting to optimize liquidity.
